analysis.one_liner: Restores the strict federal arsenic limit for drinking water and funds treatment upgrades to meet it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2001 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2003 without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2001, EPA finalized a rule tightening the limit on arsenic allowed in public drinking water (66 Fed. Reg. 6976). This bill would put that rule back into full force by statute and direct EPA to send federal money to states for treatment projects that water systems need to comply, scaled to each state's share of the need. It never moved past its first committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People served by public water systems with arsenic levels above the stricter standard — the bill would require those systems to treat water to the January 2001 EPA limit and would fund part of the cost with federal grants to states.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates, with full force of law, EPA's final rule 'Arsenic and Clarifications to Compliance and New Source Contaminants Monitoring,' published January 22, 2001.

It directs EPA to allocate funds to states for treatment projects to comply with the reinstated rule, in proportion to each state's financial need for compliance projects among all public water systems.

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems that exceed the stricter arsenic standard — and their ratepayers — bear treatment costs, offset by federal grants that depend on Congress providing money each year.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small water systems in areas with naturally high arsenic, and those costs are typically passed on through water bills.

The federal assistance is conditional: money is allocated only 'for each fiscal year for which funds are made available,' so the bill provides no guaranteed funding for the systems it requires to treat their water.
A statutory mandate leaves regulators less flexibility to phase in or adjust the standard than the normal EPA rulemaking process provides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong — arsenic in drinking water is a known cancer risk, and the bill both restores the limit and helps states pay for compliance. The honest weakness is the funding: systems are required to treat, but the federal help depends on yearly appropriations, so small systems and their ratepayers could be left carrying much of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on March 27, 2001, with introductory remarks, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill.
The bill would reinstate EPA's January 2001 arsenic rule with full force and effect and allocate federal funds to states for treatment projects to comply with it.
No further action appears in the record after the committee referral; the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without the bill ever reaching a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water systems that would have faced treatment costs under the reinstated standard avoided the bill's requirements — though the bill's narrow cosponsor base and early committee referral meant it never had a realistic path regardless.

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 27, 2001 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only legislators on record were the Democratic sponsor and his three Democratic cosponsors, so no partisan breakdown of support or opposition exists.

industries.note: The bill would force systems exceeding the January 2001 arsenic limit to install treatment, with costs borne by the systems and their ratepayers. Systems with naturally high arsenic — often small rural systems — would bear the most, partially offset by federal grants.
The bill authorizes federal money to help states fund arsenic treatment projects, a cost to taxpayers in exchange for safer drinking water. Funding is tied to annual appropriations.
